extracted.intended_audience: small business representatives, policy analysts, labor/employment attorneys, and stakeholders responding to DOL rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Estimating and analyzing the impacts of a DOL overtime/EAP rule on small entities pursuant to the Regulatory Flexibility Act, including data sources, assumptions, alternative scenarios, and updating mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Significant economic impact determination (percent of payroll/revenue threshold)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the rule will have a 'significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities'—assessed using measures such as costs and payroll increases as a percent of payroll and percent of revenues (SBA Advocacy referenced a one to three percent of revenue threshold).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Department calculates compliance cost and increased wages as a percent of payroll and translates to percent of revenues; reported results (e.g., less than 0.9% of payroll and less than 0.2% of revenues per affected small entity, with industry exceptions) are used to conclude impacts are unlikely to be significant. See referenced Tables (e.g., Table 32, Table 34).

rubrics_metrics.name: Enterprise coverage and treatment of nonprofits
rubrics_metrics.description: When determining enterprise coverage, only revenue derived from business operations, not charitable activities, is included; however, workers employed by enterprises that do not meet enterprise coverage requirements were nonetheless included in estimates of workers subject to the FLSA due to lack of data to exclude them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because no adequate data set exists to identify and exclude enterprises that fail enterprise coverage, the Department includes those workers in population estimates—acknowledging this may overestimate impacts, particularly for nonprofits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of non-quantifiable, non-financial effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-financial consequences (e.g., worker flexibility, worker morale, loss of benefits, career advancement) should be identified and addressed even if not quantified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Department discusses these possible impacts qualitatively (see sections V.B.4.v and VII.C.3.v) but did not quantify costs regarding scheduling flexibility due to little data or literature; cites empirical studies (e.g., Golden using GSS) that inform but do not provide quantification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compliance options and practical employer responses
rubrics_metrics.description: Employers do not need to reclassify nonexempt workers as hourly employees; they may pay overtime premium for hours over 40, or continue to pay a salary provided the salary equates to a base hourly wage at least equal to minimum wage and overtime premium is paid for overtime hours.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Department emphasizes options (pay overtime on a salaried basis, maintain benefits, allow flexible scheduling under employer timekeeping rules) and notes that reductions in benefits are not necessarily required to offset payroll increases given estimated modest impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration and analysis of regulatory alternatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Department must describe regulatory alternatives considered (e.g., lower/higher salary thresholds, phased increases) and explain why chosen thresholds were selected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department considered several alternatives in the NPRM and in the final rule and explains why it set the selected standard salary level and HCE total compensation requirement (including use of lowest-wage Census Region). SBA Advocacy's suggested alternatives were considered and responded to.

rubrics_metrics.name: Updating mechanism for earnings thresholds (lawfulness and predictability)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of a triennial updating mechanism that resets thresholds using current BLS earnings data at a fixed percentile, without requiring a separate notice-and-comment rulemaking for each update.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Department explains methodology and defends lawfulness: future updates apply current data to an already-established regulatory standard; will publish notice with revised thresholds not fewer than 150 days before effectiveness; argues mechanism yields more predictable, incremental changes versus irregular updates and rebuts 'ratcheting' concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data source selection and vintage (use of SUSB, NAICS, SBA size standards)
rubrics_metrics.description: Primary data source for estimating small entities and employment is the Statistics of U.S. Businesses (SUSB); SBA entity size standards (2019) and 2017 data are used to align with SUSB breakdowns; alternative sources used where asset thresholds apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Department used 2017 data where possible (to align with 2017 SUSB), applied 2019 SBA standards, used alternative sources for asset-threshold industries (credit unions, banks, agriculture, public administration), and aggregated 6-digit NAICS into 27 industry categories to maintain sample sizes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling of data bins and distribution assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: If an SBA size cutoff falls in the middle of a SUSB bracket/category, assume a uniform distribution of employees across that bracket to apportion establishments as small or not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This assumption is used to determine proportions of firms/establishments considered small when discrete bracket boundaries don't align with SBA cutoffs; those proportions were then applied to more recent counts (e.g., 2021 SUSB) to estimate current small establishments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method to assign exempt/affected workers to small entities
rubrics_metrics.description: Assume the probability that an exempt EAP worker in CPS data is employed by a small entity equals the proportion of all workers in the corresponding industry employed by small entities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because no data indicate small businesses are more or less likely to employ exempt/affected EAP workers, the Department applies industry-level small-entity employment shares to the population of exempt EAP workers to estimate counts employed by small entities (producing e.g., 1.6M of 4.3M affected workers employed by small entities).

rubrics_metrics.name: Range estimation approach for number of affected small entities
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide upper- and lower-bound estimates using alternative distributional assumptions: (a) at most one affected worker per small entity (upper-end count of affected entities), and (b) all employees at an entity affected using average small-entity size (lower-end count of affected entities).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This yields a range (e.g., between 208,300 and 1.6 million affected small entities), and clarifies how impacts per entity vary inversely with the number of affected employees per entity; presents average affected employees per establishment under the 'all employees affected' method and one affected employee per establishment under the other.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of impacts to estimate for small entities
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimate various impact categories on small entities including regulatory familiarization costs, adjustment costs, managerial costs, and payroll increases borne by employers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Department presents these categories and quantifies them where possible (expressed as percent of payroll and revenue), providing tables by industry and employer type to illustrate distributions and magnitudes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of private households and excluded populations
rubrics_metrics.description: Private households are excluded from the analysis due to lack of data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department explicitly omits private households from the SUSB-based estimates because of insufficient data; notes other limitations where data do not disaggregate entities by revenue sizes or enterprise coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industry aggregation and handling of sample-size limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Aggregate 6-digit NAICS results to a coarser set (27 industry categories) when necessary to maintain adequate sample sizes for estimation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Department started with a 51-industry breakdown and aggregated where necessary; uses industry- and employer-type (nonprofit/for-profit/government) breakdowns and presents tables by aggregated industry categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expressing impacts relative to payroll and revenue (translation methodology)
rubrics_metrics.description: Express compliance costs and wage impacts as percentages of payroll and translate to approximate percentages of revenues, using the proportionality that payroll is largely proportionate to number of employees and that revenues are a multiple of payroll (industry varying).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Department calculates percent-of-payroll impacts and then notes that those will be less than or equal to corresponding percent-of-revenue impacts (e.g., if costs are 2% of payroll, costs will be less than 2% of revenues), and reports specific industry examples (e.g., food services payroll impacts and corresponding revenue percent).

rubrics_metrics.name: Provision of small entity compliance assistance
rubrics_metrics.description: Publish a small entity compliance guide and provide technical assistance to help employers comply with the FLSA rule, pursuant to SBREFA section 212.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Department commits to publishing the compliance guide and issuing technical assistance; notes that industry associations often provide compliance help to members and that Department will provide materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective date and phased applicability for thresholds
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt delayed applicability dates and staged initial thresholds to provide time for compliance; e.g., final higher thresholds not applicable until ~8 months after publication; initial lower thresholds set for an interim period and later updated on July 1, 2024.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Department explains the selected delayed applicability, initial threshold values ($844/week initial, then higher later), and rationale—addressing commenter requests for 1–18 month delays and balancing preparation time against timely implementation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of RFA timing requirements for scheduled updates
rubrics_metrics.description: RFA requires a regulatory flexibility analysis to accompany any agency final rule promulgated under 5 U.S.C. 553; Department interprets that it need not conduct a new RFA before each scheduled update under an established updating mechanism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Department estimates costs of future triennial updates using the fixed percentile method in this analysis and asserts that commenters did not cite RFA language requiring a new RFA for each update; explains that RFA applies to rulemaking and the initial rule includes the updating mechanism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment of administrative burden, predictability, and employer ability to anticipate updates
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether the updating mechanism imposes ongoing administrative burdens or instead provides predictability by allowing employers to track BLS earnings data quarterly to estimate future threshold changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Department contrasts regular, pre-determined triennial updates using public BLS data (allowing employers to estimate changes) with irregular updates that could be larger and less predictable; commits to publishing notice 150 days before changes to enhance predictability.
